articles.title: Punishment alone won’t help gang-involved teens – a former child soldier explains why
articles.author: Charles Wratto, Non-Resident Research Fellow, Igbinedion University Okada
paras: When Americans hear of child soldiers, they may imagine tragic images of children wielding rifles on distant battlefields.
But the conditions that help warlords recruit children into armed conflict abroad also help gang leaders draw young people into violent organizations in the U.S.

In cities across the country, gang violence continues to claim lives and fracture communities. A September 2025 FBI report recorded 69,273 incidents involving gang activity – most often assaults – between 2021 and 2024. Young people ages 13 to 16 were the most frequently reported offenders.
Policy responses to this crisis have largely focused on policing, prosecution and tougher penalties. Those responses cost federal, state and local governments billions of dollars annually.
Far less attention is paid to why violence offers some young people a sense of purpose, belonging and identity in the first place.

Gang-involved youth in the U.S. are not child soldiers in a legal or conventional sense, and American gangs are not rebel or insurgent groups. Nonetheless, the ways some young Americans become embedded in violent organizations – and the difficulty of leaving them – overlap remarkably with the child soldier experience.

As a former child soldier who is now a peace and conflict studies researcher, I have lived through organized violence and have since studied how violence shapes young people’s relationships, identities and opportunities. This work has led me to ask how decades of research on child soldier recruitment and reintegration might help young Americans caught in gang violence.
Recruitment is not always coercion

Research on child recruitment – and my own peacebuilding work, including negotiating the release of abducted children in Mali, South Sudan and northern Nigeria – shows that children are not always forced into armed groups at gunpoint. Their pathways into such groups cannot be understood as the result of coercion alone.

Armed groups may reach children through peers, community networks, relatives or other social connections. In places marked by insecurity and limited opportunities, children may not make a single decision to enter violence. Rather, relationships and constrained choices can draw them closer until entry seems like a viable way to gain a perceived sense of security and control over their own lives.

In many American cities, gang involvement follows a similar path: A 2025 study of 1,808 male adolescents in Multnomah County, Oregon, who have been referred to the juvenile justice system, found that exposure to gang-involved peers and relatives was associated with a greater likelihood of gang membership.

Through social networks, as well as music and online culture, gangs can project status, power and recognition. For young people who feel excluded by peers or disconnected in school, or who face instability at home, these signals can make gang involvement appear to offer something immediate and tangible: safety, identity and belonging. Researchers have found that some young people also join partly for protection, even though gang members face a higher risk of victimization than their peers.

Social media has intensified these dynamics, spreading images of violence, wealth, weapons and notoriety far beyond the neighborhoods and front lines where gangs and armed groups operate. The conflict in Sudan offers a stark example: Young fighters have been publicly celebrated and stylized online, including in videos portraying youngsters in military uniform as heroic “lion cubs” and in AI-generated clips placing them beside senior commanders.
Young people in both gangs and armed groups may feel a sense of safety, connection and recognition. But what a young person sees as belonging can become a powerful mechanism of control.

Gang leaders in urban communities, like warlords in conflict zones, often position themselves as providers, protectors, mentors and father figures. They impose rules, settle disputes, reward loyalty and regulate access to opportunity and protection. For marginalized youth, they offer recognition where there is isolation, structure where there is instability and identity where there is exclusion.
That world gives young people purpose and belonging, but both are conditional on loyalty, obedience and participation, which makes leaving difficult even when the risks of staying become clear.
Why punishment alone falls short
Arrests and incarceration can interrupt violence, but they do not necessarily dismantle the systems that draw young people into gangs.

As in conflict settings – where removing children from armed groups does not eliminate commanders, recruiters, networks or incentives – incarcerating young Americans can remove participants from the street without disrupting the structures, relationships or conditions that lured them to gang involvement. When they are released, those same influences may remain, making a return more likely.

This does not mean that young offenders should not be held accountable for violent acts they commit. But evidence from juveniles convicted of serious offenses, including felonies, suggests that punishment beyond what is necessary for public safety does not produce greater deterrence. Young people are rarely the architects of the systems that exploit them. When accountability is directed primarily at the young person at the bottom of that structure, the organization itself can remain intact.

Global prosecutions for child soldier recruitment have largely focused on commanders who direct and exploit children. Likewise, reducing youth violence requires attention to those who organize it, not only those caught in it. If a gang’s leadership, or the networks that profit from it, remain in place, billions spent deterring young offenders will not protect American streets or the children who walk them.
One of the hardest lessons from helping child soldiers return to their communities is that leaving violence does not mean the transition is complete.

Children who leave armed groups are often disarmed, demobilized and provided with vocational training, education and material assistance. But training someone to make a living is different from creating the conditions – a functioning market, infrastructure, mentorship and networks – in which that person can succeed.

For example, when a young person sells the sewing machine or other equipment that a reintegration program gave them to earn a living, it can look like a personal failure. But if the economic environment is unfavorable, or the infrastructure and support systems needed to sustain that new livelihood are absent, those shortcomings may explain the outcome as much as individual decisions do.

A 16-year study in Mozambique found that long-term reintegration of ex-child soldiers was shaped by livelihoods, sustained support, forgiveness and community acceptance. This has a direct lesson for the U.S.: A young person can leave a gang or come home from incarceration and return to a society that primarily sees them as an offender.

A 2021 study conducted across 12 U.S. states found that people with juvenile records face significant barriers to education, credentialing and meaningful employment. Another study found that a juvenile record can hurt an applicant’s employment opportunities.
If the neighborhood, family and institutions around that young person have not changed, the conditions that made violence attractive remain, and stigma can become a mechanism of re-recruitment.
The U.S. does not need to replicate child soldier reintegration programs, but it can learn from their successes and failures.

Removing young people from violent organizations is only part of the solution. The real measure of success is whether there are legitimate alternatives to the social world that violence provides and whether society can hold young people accountable while still creating pathways for them to build new lives.
Charles Wratto is affiliated with the Center for Peace and Violence Prevention (CPVP).

articles.title: Why your vote for local chief prosecutor will matter on Election Day
articles.author: Ronald Wright, Professor of Criminal Law, Wake Forest University
paras: Before most Americans step into the voting booth in November, they will already know their choices at the top of the ballot, in races for governor, the Senate and House of Representatives. But a race near the bottom of the ballot – for the chief prosecutor in their local district – will probably affect the voters’ lives more directly.
As a former prosecutor and as a scholar of the criminal courts for over three decades, I have seen how local district attorneys take the lead in responding to crime. This vote matters.

The chief prosecutor in local criminal courts – the titles vary, such as district attorney, prosecuting attorney, state’s attorney or county attorney – has enormous discretionary power over criminal law enforcement.

While state legislators pass the statutes that define crimes, local prosecutors decide where to spend limited enforcement dollars. They decide which cases to file and work with the police to address the crimes that matter most in each county.
Prosecutors also choose how to negotiate guilty pleas. While judges select criminal sentences in each case, prosecutors influence that choice with their own recommended sentence.
No official matters more than the chief prosecutor when it comes to using the resources of the courts and prisons.
Until the early 2010s, party labels did not matter in these local races, because Republicans and Democrats backed similar priorities. Prison was the central tool at every prosecutor’s disposal.

The prosecutor’s job centered on charging as many people as possible with crimes that could result in the longest possible prison term. Convictions for less serious crimes were valuable ways to build the defendant’s criminal record, making it easy to obtain prison sentences in the future.

Democratic and Republican candidates figured that voters wanted them to be “tough on crime.” Because the easiest way to send that signal was to press for more prisons, the size and cost of prisons mushroomed for decades.
And because most prosecutors presented the same basic options to voters, incumbents usually ran unopposed. Even when opposed, they beat the challengers in most races.
Over the past 10 to 15 years, however, prosecutor candidates have offered voters some real choices.

In King County, Washington, for example, voters in 2022 chose a candidate who emphasized prevention and mental health services alongside traditional criminal prosecutions. Her opponent had instead promised to file more criminal cases.

Voters today have more power to decide how many jail cells they want to fund and use. More traditional prosecutor candidates might continue to focus on prisons in their responses to crime, relying on its presumed power to incapacitate criminals.

This was the campaign strategy of a 2025 challenger in Norfolk, Virginia, who called for a return to heavier prison use after four years of efforts by the incumbent to reduce incarceration. Voters rejected this proposal and returned the incumbent to office.

Reform-oriented prosecutors, such as the district attorney in Milwaukee, are depending on less expensive nonprison punishments, including treatment programs for a wider range of crimes, reserving prison for more serious violent offenses. These reordered priorities seem to work as designed. They reduce prison use without increasing crime rates.

These reform-oriented prosecutors, like the county attorney in Minneapolis, might also develop diversion programs, sending some defendants into community service programs. Typically, prosecutors offer diversion to defendants under age 18. Some offices, such as the Pima County attorney in Arizona, offer diversion to adults accused of less serious crimes.
Some prosecutors, like the district attorney in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, design and lead some of these programs themselves. Often they partner with nonprofit groups that promote public safety.

Prosecutor candidates also give voters choices on which defendants to hold in the local jail, at public expense, while their charges are pending. Some offices have reduced or eliminated the use of cash bail, without increasing local crime. Candidates also give voters choices about new approaches to victim support services and programs designed to improve the reentry of convicted people into the community.

Apart from the various options that prosecutor candidates can offer, voters can expect prosecutors to work transparently. Candidates can commit to routinely releasing data about office operations. That’s what the Democratic candidate did in her successful race for commonwealth attorney in Arlington, Virginia. That data can allow journalists and researchers to evaluate trends over time, not just information about individual cases.

There are many offices – such as Jacksonville, Florida, and Boulder, Colorado – that show their work on data dashboards. That transparency allows the public to judge, between elections, how well the prosecutor delivers on campaign promises.

Recent political trends show that prosecutor elections are becoming more competitive, with more incumbents facing challengers. These races are also being driven by politics at the national level, as voters increasingly elect prosecutor candidates from the same party they prefer in national and state offices.
In this changing environment, I believe it’s worth voters’ time to explore expanded options in prosecutor races.

articles.title: What legal experts say about the Trump administration’s attempts to make a federal case out of state elections
articles.author: Naomi Schalit, Politics and Legal Affairs Editor, The Conversation
paras: The Trump administration’s lawsuit against Alaska, which seeks to block certification of the U.S. Senate results there if the GOP candidate does not win, is the latest in a long series of actions throughout 2026 in which the administration has attempted to wrest control of federal elections from states.

In the Alaska case, the U.S. Department of Justice, directed by President Donald Trump, claims that it aims to “protect the integrity of the 2026 Senate election in Alaska.” If incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan does not win reelection in a close vote, the DOJ asserts, it’s likely the result of voter confusion because another candidate with a very similar name – Daniel J. Sullivan, with no party affiliation – is on the ballot, too. So in the event that Sen. Sullivan fails to win reelection, the DOJ demands that Alaska not certify the election and instead should conduct an inquest into who voters thought they were voting for.

The campaign of the Democratic candidate, Mary Peltola, whose potential win in the hotly contested election could help shift the Senate to Democratic control, has called the lawsuit “wholly baseless” and “an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections” in a court filing. Another filing states that the DOJ lawsuit “asks the Court to preemptively nullify Alaska’s U.S. Senate election and disenfranchise Alaska voters without any legal basis whatsoever. It seeks to go where law ends.”

There’s lots of other heated language in the case’s legal filings. But colorful language and legal citations are a much longer way of articulating a simple fact: The U.S. Constitution gives the president no authority over federal elections. That authority rests with the states and, to a limited degree, with Congress.
Over the past year, as the 2026 midterm elections approached, The Conversation has published a number of stories illustrating this fundamental constitutional rule. Here is a selection of them:
1. The Constitution bars presidential control

“States are empowered under Article 1, Section 4, of the Constitution to conduct elections and set the time, place and manner of those elections,” former federal judge John E. Jones told The Conversation in an interview on April 22, 2026. Jones was discussing Trump’s March 31 executive order to take control of mail-in voting from states and give it to the U.S. Postal Service and the Department of Homeland Security.
Jones, who is now the president of Dickinson College, explained why the framers of the Constitution set up a process in which states run elections and not the federal government:

“First of all, the federal government didn’t have the apparatus to conduct elections. And states had been running elections; they knew how to do it. There was a great deal of trust in the states’ ability to run elections. And there was the core debate of federalism, as to what powers states could retain, and they didn’t want to abdicate many of those powers,” Jones said.

There was also, Jones added, “a debate about the potential for fraud, that if there was a single entity controlling all the elections – that is, if you centralize elections under one politically motivated executive – it’s a really fraught situation which can be abused.”

“The Constitution is clear,” said Jones. “Unless amended, Article 1, Section 4 is – to use the trite phrase – what it is. The power rests with the states, absent congressional action. There is no mention of the president. None.”
2. Limits on Congress, too
The Republican-controlled House also tried this year to horn in on the constitutional power of states to regulate elections and who can vote.

In February 2026, the House, urged by Trump, passed the SAVE America Act. The act would have required those registering to vote in federal elections to – in person – “provide documentary proof of U.S. citizenship.” It also required some people who were voting in federal elections to give proof of U.S. citizenship.

John J. Martin, an election law scholar at Quinnipiac University Law School, wrote that the act “presents a constitutional dilemma. By requiring individuals to show documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to vote, the SAVE America Act is implicitly saying that someone must be a U.S. citizen to vote in federal elections.”

In other words, Martin wrote, “Congress would be instituting a qualification to vote, a power that the Constitution leaves exclusively to the states. Normally, when state and federal laws conflict, the Constitution’s supremacy clause mandates that federal law prevails. Yet, in this instance, where Congress has no actual authority to implement voter qualifications, the SAVE America Act would seem to have no constitutional leg on which to stand.”
The Senate proved unwilling to pass the SAVE Act this year, so this particular constitutional battle has yet to hit the courts.
3. A bar on federal limits to mail voting – so far

Trump frequently targets mail voting, claiming it’s rife with fraud. The March 2026 executive order by the president aimed, it said, to ensure “integrity in federal elections” by placing severe restrictions on mail voting.

Among that order’s provisions was a directive to the U.S. Postal Service to implement, election scholar Martin wrote, “uniform ballot and envelope requirements for mail and absentee ballots used in federal elections.” The order also mandated that states must “provide the Postal Service, 60 days prior to Election Day, with lists of all voters eligible to vote by mail or absentee.”

A mail ballot that didn’t comply with the Postal Service’s requirements, or was sent by somebody not on a state-provided list, would not be delivered by the Postal Service, wrote Martin, “effectively canceling that vote.”
Lawsuits were filed by a host of state officials and voting rights groups. The suits eventually made their way up to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Martin summarized their arguments: “The president does not possess unilateral authority to alter the methods of voting in federal elections. Rather, the elections clause of the Constitution vests the authority to regulate the ‘time, place, and manner’ of federal elections in the states. Congress also has the authority to regulate federal elections, if it chooses to do so.”
On Sept. 14, 2026, the Supreme Court apparently agreed, with a 7-2 vote upholding a preliminary injunction blocking the new rules.

articles.title: Data centers are inspiring bipartisanship – for now
articles.author: Barbara A. Trish, Professor of Political Science, Grinnell College
paras: It may not be as shocking as rogue AI agents hacking another system, but the current political resistance to data centers has taken a surprising turn: It’s bringing together strange bedfellows, from democratic socialist Sen. Bernie Sanders to right-wing strategist Steve Bannon.

Organized opposition to new data centers, made up of a coalition of varied interests, has spread across the nation. Through protests, packed zoning commission meetings, moratoriums and other government action, the resistance has upended dozens of proposed projects.

Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. They’re also massive facilities that require extraordinary amounts of energy. By 2030, U.S. data center electricity use is expected to reach 12% of the nation’s total consumption.

They carry some benefits. At the national level, data centers fuel the computing power seen as critical to U.S. competition with China. Locally, they create an uptick in jobs, especially during the construction phase, and can generate tax revenue. In the lead-up to the 2026 midterm elections, though, the heavy costs associated with them – such as land use, higher household utility bills and environmental degradation – appear to outweigh the benefits, bringing together people who usually find themselves politically at odds.

I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of AI in political campaigns is reshaping established practices and power dynamics. I believe data centers may be disrupting some of the partisan issue alignments Americans have grown to expect.
Political disruption – AI style

Despite ongoing debate about the extent of and reasons for polarization, one thing is for sure: Democrats and Republicans stake out distinct positions on many issues. Pew Research Center data shows, for example, that 63% of Democrats say climate change is a very big problem facing the country, compared with 14% of Republicans, a 49-point gap.

By contrast, the partisan gap on data centers is small – and getting smaller: In summer 2026, the Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans whether they support the construction of data centers in their communities. Supporters of both parties were more opposed than supportive, although opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%. That partisan gap had narrowed over the previous four months, moving from 18 to 15 points.

This year has been marked by considerable upheaval: political, economic and technological. Americans have been hit hard with surging fuel and energy prices. And with rapid AI development, they witness real-world examples of the sort of lapses in safety that have worried both AI insiders and observers.

One “rogue” attack announced in July 2026 involved OpenAI’s AI agents escaping a secure environment and autonomously – without human direction or assistance – breaking into the system of Hugging Face, another AI company. Shortly after, news broke that out-of-control AI agents were not just a one-off limited to that hack.

Polling shows that majorities of both parties feel that AI technology is developing too fast, though Democrats’ levels of concern are 22 points higher than Republicans’. The gap is much smaller – 4 points – on support for government keeping AI under human control and on protecting U.S. workers. Backing for each is very high, hovering around 80%.

This bipartisanship on attitudes about AI and data centers appears also to show up in alliances on the ground and, in some cases, in new organizations with a focus on thwarting data centers. For example, New York’s No Data Center FLX has organized protests, sued the local zoning board of appeals and collected almost 23,000 petition signatures in opposition to a proposed data center.

Government makes decisions about data centers at all levels. In cities and counties, zoning fights draw a disparate resistance: environmentalists, folks reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.

Some bipartisanship has extended to Congress. In mid-September, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a wide margin: 417-3. The bill requires states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs.

The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill, which would establish a voluntary structure, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Comparable sentiment killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.

As midterm elections approach, candidates up and down the ballot are blanketing the airwaves and digital channels with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump, for his part, has weighed in, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.” It’s a fine line for some Republican candidates between responding to voter concerns and not alienating the president.

If data center politics seem familiar, it may be because this isn’t the first issue to bring together such a diverse coalition: In the 1990s, opposition to the North American Free Trade Agreement did the same, uniting organized labor and environmentalists, frequent adversaries, over concerns about job losses and pollution. That alliance never extended beyond the boundaries of its singular focus on trade agreements, though. Similarly, don’t expect data centers to permanently reshape the U.S. political landscape.

articles.title: Congress is freeing Trump of the limited legal requirements left on him by the Supreme Court
articles.author: Stephanie A. (Sam) Martin, Frank and Bethine Church Endowed Chair of Public Affairs, Boise State University
paras: On the evening of Oct. 11, just weeks before the 2026 midterm elections, a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to stop airing taxpayer-funded television advertisements praising President Donald Trump.
Yet two of the ads continued running past the court’s deadline, including during broadcasts of “60 Minutes” and “ABC World News Tonight.”

The commercials in question aired in violation of a decades-old congressional prohibition against using federal money for unauthorized publicity and propaganda. Yet Republican congressional leaders did little to stop the president’s ad spending. That left outside organizations and a political candidate to challenge them in federal court.

The episode illustrates a larger development in Trump’s second presidency. Across disputes involving federal spending, government agencies and military operations, the administration has asserted authority that is either restricted by law or that the legislative branch has reserved for itself.
But responsibility for enforcing those limits is increasingly falling to organizations, institutions and individuals outside of the legislative branch.
As a scholar of the American presidency and deliberative democracy, I pay close attention to how the nation’s chief executive exercises power and communicates with the public.
When presidents are allowed to break rules and disregard democratic norms without consequence, I worry that citizens will grow cynical and lose faith in the idea of self-government.

As this happens, citizens may come to see the law as something that applies selectively, depending on who holds power, and lose confidence in the institutions responsible for holding their leaders accountable.
They may also begin to accept the absence of accountability as a normal feature of political life, weakening the public expectations on which democratic government depends.
Congress is not the only branch of government demurring from holding the president accountable.
In July 2024, the Supreme Court provided presidents sweeping protection from criminal prosecution for actions taken in office under the “core constitutional powers” of the position.

In “Trump v. United States,” the court held that former presidents cannot be criminally prosecuted for actions taken under powers the Constitution gives exclusively to the president. Along with this “absolute immunity,” the justices also granted “at least presumptive immunity” for other official acts.

In their decision, the court’s conservative majority extended the meaning of official conduct to the “outer perimeter” of presidential responsibilities and prohibited courts from examining a president’s motives when determining whether an act was official.

The ruling only addressed criminal liability and did not curtail Congress’ constitutional authority to investigate presidential conduct, control federal spending, enact statutory restrictions and, in serious cases, pursue impeachment.
Yet the Republican majority in Congress has largely declined to exercise these powers against Trump, in areas ranging from declaring war to spending money.

Their acquiescence is helping create a new form of official protection, which I call “practical immunity.” In using this term, I am borrowing from the work of scholars who study abuse in the American penal system.

Those thinkers argue that legal obstacles, institutional hesitation and political incentives sometimes make it difficult to hold public officials accountable, even when the law suggests there has been illegal conduct.
That is what appears to be increasingly happening now with Congress, the courts and the president.
When Congress stops defending its laws
The television ads case illustrates the conundrum of practical immunity.

In opposing the temporary restraining order, the Trump administration’s attorneys did not contest the argument asserted by the plaintiffs – Common Cause and two unions – that the expenditures violated federal appropriations law. Instead, they said the plaintiffs lacked standing to sue. They also argued that the case was moot because the advertising campaign was ending.

Those arguments failed in court. Yet the administration’s defense demonstrated how elusive enforcing a law can be when Congress fails to assert its constitutionally granted role, even when the underlying legal restriction is clear. To win, a plaintiff must establish a concrete injury and persuade a judge to intervene. While this happens, the disputed conduct often continues.
In this case, the president went on spending public money in violation of the law. The GOP-led Congress, meanwhile, remained silent, even though its own role was being usurped.

Another boundary that Trump has repeatedly tested is the so-called “power of the purse”, which is among the legislative branch’s most important constitutional responsibilities. Presidents may spend federal money only for purposes Congress has authorized. The Impoundment Control Act of 1974 protects lawmakers’ decisions against presidential efforts to ignore congressional appropriations.

In September 2026, Trump’s administration canceled more than US$800 million in congressionally approved spending for immigrant services, climate change and civil rights for minority groups. The cancellation was done through a maneuver known as a pocket rescission. The administration timed its action to make it difficult for Congress to consider or stop the rescission. The Government Accountability Office – an independent agency that examines how taxpayer dollars are spent – said tactics like these violate federal law.
When this happened, a few members of Congress tried to intervene and stop the rescission, but the Republican majority blocked their efforts.
The collapse of institutional rivalry
The separation of powers divides authority among the legislative, executive and judicial branches of government to prevent too much power from becoming concentrated in any one place.

The architects of the Constitution anticipated that officials in different branches would compete to preserve their authority. In Federalist No. 51, James Madison argued that maintaining the balance established by the separation of powers depended on the ambitions of public officials coming into conflict. Members of Congress could be expected to resist presidential encroachments because those encroachments diminished their own power.
Fierce partisanship has complicated this arrangement.

Legal scholars Daryl Levinson and Richard Pildes have shown how political competition mostly now happens inside and between parties, rather than among branches of government. When one party controls Congress and the presidency, legislators may become more invested in advancing their party’s agenda than they are in defending their institution’s constitutional authority.

Trump’s influence over Republican voters intensifies these incentives. Lawmakers who oppose him risk public ridicule, primary challenges and diminished political support. Defending congressional authority may therefore carry greater immediate – and personal – political costs than allowing presidential power to expand.
The result is a political system in which a president can act in ways that may violate federal law, undermine democratic norms and encroach on Congress’ constitutional authority.

Madison’s constitutional design assumed that public officials would defend the powers entrusted to them. The danger to the American constitutional system emerging in Trump’s second term is that congressional leaders have begun to regard those powers as expendable, allowing the president to exercise authority under conditions of practical immunity. He faces little fear of meaningful institutional consequences.

articles.title: Andy Burnham has maintained the public’s approval through his first 100 days as the UK’s PM – that’s unheard of these days
articles.author: Stephen Coleman, Emeritus Professor of Political Communication, University of Leeds
paras: In his first 100 days in office, Andy Burnham has challenged the economic consensus shared by UK governments in recent decades and set up a prime ministerial office outside London with a remit to rewire the state and devolve power. He has also reopened the debate on Brexit and set in motion the biggest social house-building programme since the post-war period.

These are big moves for the prime minister, not unlike those proposed in the king’s speech a month after the 1945 Labour landslide. Then, the Attlee government set out a blueprint focused on nationalising key industries, creating a universal health service and expanding social security.

In some ways, the political bar today is not set very high. Burnham has been preceded by six prime ministers in ten years: Theresa May (1,106 days), constantly undermined by her own MPs; Boris Johnson (1,140 days), destroyed by his own dishonesty; Liz Truss (49 days), now a byword for policy disaster; Rishi Sunak (619 days), the leader behind the biggest Tory electoral defeat ever; and Keir Starmer (717 days), who conjured broad unpopularity out of a landslide election victory.

Burnham’s first task in office was therefore simply to look like he could stay there. His second task was to build upon one of the largest parliamentary majorities (currently 158) in the past century. Doing so has meant making big moves.

The most potent message that voters have sent to all politicians and parties is that they want to see tangible change. They are tired of austerity in its various versions; of relentless national decline; of the political state appearing to be incapable of delivering anything worthwhile; of having to live with the bad decisions of the past; and of identikit politicians who seem devoid of imagination.

In his first speech as prime minister in Downing Street on July 20, Burnham proposed “making this moment a circuit-breaker for Britain, bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years.” Not business as usual.

In his speech to the Labour party conference in September, Burnham spelled out what he meant by change. He told delegates that Britain had been on the “wrong path” for years, citing deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity and Brexit. He said this had created a country “run for vested interests” rather than in the public interest, stating that he was ready to do things his predecessors would not.

In that short section of the speech, he separated himself from both the policies and the stylistics of his six predecessors. First, in speaking about the past 40 years he was clearly referring to an era in which every policy, need and sentiment has had to defer to the rationale of the market. To challenge neoliberal doctrine in these times is in itself an act of radicalism.

Second, by stating openly that Brexit was an economic disaster he distanced himself from the isolationist fantasy to which UK prime ministers have felt forced to adhere since 2016. In a world of dangerously unreliable geopolitical blocs, renegotiating the settlement with European neighbours would point to a new relationship with reality.

Third, references in the same speech to “power held in too few hands” and the promise of a “new politics” speak to the possibility of decentralised state power. They also signal a fairer method of determining who will wield it. Such boldness has not marked the first 100 days of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher in 1979. Back then, proposals to sell off nationalised industries, break trade union power and give the market free rein within her first 100 days laid the groundwork for what would become Thatcherism.

Of course, the power to enact these big changes is not entirely in Burnham’s hands. In agreeing to stay within the fiscal rules established by its predecessors, as well as to meet the Nato target for defence spending, the new government is extremely constrained in how much money it can invest in public services.

The bond markets, traditionally hostile to the risk they perceive around policies shaped by social justice, stand as a threat to radicalism. The right-wing press has lost no time in casting Burnham as (alternately) incompetent and dangerous.

And at his heels, in the shape of Reform UK, is a mega-funded populist party. Its reputation and poll ratings are currently diminished, but it is constantly waiting in the wings to exploit any deflation of public mood.

That said, after 100 days Burnham remains the most popular party leader in the UK. His 46% approval rating comfortably beats those of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch (33%), Reform’s Nigel Farage (25%) and Ed Davey of the Liberal Democrats (24%). This is the longest period in nearly ten years that a prime minister has gone without recording a negative net favourability rating. The British electorate is not used to feeling approval. Let’s see if it lasts.

articles.title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear
articles.author: Monique Mitchell Turner, Professor of Communication, Michigan State University
paras: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.

The ad ran as a paid spot only once, in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater. The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war. Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news.

I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out, and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear, and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.
Fear is an alarm. It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.

When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.

During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical. Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.

Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.

More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it.

Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.
The critical ingredient is empowerment

Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead. They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem.

For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.

My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information. Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.

Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.
Fear plays on prejudice and stereotypes
Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.

One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.

Bush’s campaign followed up with the “Revolving Door” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes.

Political scientist Tali Mendelberg’s research described in “The Race Card” shows that these implicit appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful. But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.
Gender works in a similar way.

In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher Mirya Holman and colleagues found that when campaign messages triggered fears of terrorism, voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as tough on security.

A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability for Muslim candidates.
Is fear a more common tactic now?
Using fear as a campaign tool is nothing new.

In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism. Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “Bear” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that seniors’ Medicare was at risk.

What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 documents that rise, though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.

The current media landscape shifts this dynamic significantly; while traditional nightly news broadcasts have seen a decline in viewership, targeted social media feeds have become the emotional battleground.

Recent digital campaign data shows that negative ads are highly prized online because they successfully grab attention by provoking strong emotions like fear and anger. Because platform recommendation systems are heavily driven by user activity, campaigns are incentivized to use emotionally charged appeals to maximize viral engagement across feeds.

Fear works less like a switch and more like a spotlight. It grabs attention and opens minds to change, but whether that turns into a vote, a boycott of the ballot box or resentment toward the messenger depends on what comes next.

articles.title: For Andy Burnham, getting closer to the EU could prove as tricky as exiting it – an expert explains
articles.author: Monika Brusenbauch Meislová, Visiting Professor, School of Law and Social Sciences, Aston University
paras: Andy Burnham has reopened a debate that successive UK prime ministers tried to settle. But the history of Brexit suggests that getting closer to the European Union may prove just as difficult as leaving it.

For years, prime ministers have attempted to put Brexit behind them. Burnham has just done the opposite. By suggesting that Britain could “go all the way” and rejoin the EU, he has broken with the cautious approach of his predecessors.
His intervention has brought renewed urgency to the question: how close should Britain remain to the EU, and on what terms?

The options are not new. From Theresa May’s attempts to secure a bespoke deal to Boris Johnson’s hard Brexit, Rishi Sunak’s pragmatism and Keir Starmer’s reset, governments have grappled with essentially the same dilemma. That is, how can the country retain the benefits of cooperation with the EU without accepting the obligations that come with it?
May: trying to have it both ways

Theresa May entered Downing Street with the task of delivering Brexit but no blueprint for doing so. Her declaration that “Brexit means Brexit” concealed a fundamental contradiction: she promised to leave the single market and customs union, end free movement and end the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice in Britain. But she also vowed to preserve close economic ties with the bloc.

May’s hopes for a bespoke deal clashed with the EU’s insistence that market access came with obligations. Her compromises satisfied neither hardline Brexit supporters nor pro-European MPs, ultimately bringing down her premiership. May’s experience exposed a dilemma that would haunt her successors. The closer Britain sought to remain to the EU, the harder it became to deliver the “control” promised by Brexit.
Johnson: getting Brexit done, but not settled

Boris Johnson offered a seemingly straightforward solution: stop searching for a compromise and embrace a more distant relationship. His promise to “get Brexit done” helped to secure a decisive election victory in 2019. Britain formally left the EU in January 2020, followed by an agreement that preserved tariff-free trade in qualifying goods but introduced new barriers such as customs checks and additional paperwork.

Yet withdrawal did not resolve the relationship. Trading frictions and disputes over Northern Ireland kept Brexit politically alive, exposing a paradox: delivering Brexit threatened to deprive its supporters of the very issue that had mobilised them. In other words, for politicians who had built their appeal around Brexit, declaring the job done risked losing a powerful means of rallying voters. The search for new Brexit victories therefore continued long after Britain had left.
Sunak: pragmatism without rapprochement

Rishi Sunak inherited a relationship marked by confrontation and mistrust. His approach was more pragmatic. The Windsor Framework of 2023 eased tensions that surrounded Northern Ireland’s post-Brexit trading arrangements, helping to restore trust between London and Brussels.

He also secured Britain’s association with Horizon Europe, an EU funding programme for research and innovation. These were significant practical achievements, but they did not amount to a fundamental rethink on Brexit. Sunak continued to champion the opportunities of regulatory independence while seeking to repair some of the disruption caused by withdrawal.
Starmer: the limits of the reset

Keir Starmer went further, promising to reset relations with the EU after years of confrontation from Conservative PMs. The Labour government pursued closer cooperation on security, trade and regulatory matters, but retained three crucial red lines: no return to the single market, no customs union and no freedom of movement.

This created a familiar problem. Britain wanted closer economic integration while continuing to reject some of the institutional arrangements that made it possible. The controversy surrounding a proposed youth mobility scheme underlined the political sensitivities involved in even limited steps towards closer ties. The reset offered opportunities for practical improvements, but its incremental approach could not eliminate the fundamental trade-offs of being outside the EU.
Burnham: a different route or the same dilemma?

Burnham now has two broad routes. The first is to deepen cooperation without pursuing full membership. A customs union could reduce barriers to goods trade, while participation in the single market through a Norway-style arrangement would offer much closer economic integration.

But these options come with conditions. Participation in the single market would require accepting EU rules and the free movement of people, without restoring Britain’s vote over those rules. A customs union would constrain independent trade policy and could require renegotiating trade deals signed since Brexit.

The second route is more ambitious: reopening the possibility of EU membership. Rejoining would restore British participation in EU decision-making, alongside the economic benefits of membership. But accession would require the agreement of all 27 member states, negotiations over Britain’s future obligations and some level of certainty that the next UK government wouldn’t just seek to come out again. The favourable terms the UK once enjoyed could not simply be assumed. Neither route offers a painless solution.

Burnham’s intervention nevertheless marks an important change. Where previous prime ministers largely sought to manage the consequences of Brexit while defending the settlement, he has questioned whether the settlement itself should be permanent. A decade after the referendum, British politics may be returning to its original EU dilemma.

articles.title: From aristocracy to ‘assetocracy’ – how wealth has transformed the House of Lords
articles.author: Huw Macartney, Associate professor in Political Economy, University of Birmingham
paras: On April 29, 2026, the remaining hereditary peers left the House of Lords. These 92 individuals were the last vestiges of an era in which the landed aristocracy dominated the UK’s second chamber. In the recent past, as many as 800 aristocrats filled the red benches. Now though, a new financial elite appears to have taken their place.

Gradually, the dominance of the aristocrats gave way to a more meritocratic order of life peers. In 1999, Tony Blair’s government removed most of the hereditary peers; in 2026, Keir Starmer’s government finished the job. But did removing them really make the House of Lords any less elitist?

These were some of the issues I sought to explore with a team of graduate researchers at the University of Birmingham. We set about gathering what is, to the best of our knowledge, the largest-ever repository of the financial and political activities of the Lords. Over 18 months, we collected details of all the shareholdings, company directorships, landholdings, rental properties, education, attendance and speeches in the second chamber, as well as voting records for all Lords. These are presented in my new book, The Assetocracy.

What we uncovered was staggering. More than 260 peers hold multiple, individual shareholdings – stakes in listed companies – worth more than £100,000 apiece. In fact, some Lords held more than 200 individual holdings, each valued in excess of £100,000. Even assuming each asset was only worth £100,000, that would put the combined value of those shareholdings alone at more than £22 million.

Put simply, this reflects a level of wealth far beyond that of all but the richest people in Britain. In fact, 14 Lords appear in The Sunday Times Rich List of the UK’s wealthiest people, with a combined net worth of £27.8 billion.

Moreover, half of the House are landlords with rental income. And 250 peers hold one or more paid company directorship. In short, this is an extraordinary concentration of wealth at the heart of Britain’s second chamber.

The social profile of the Lords is equally revealing. Nearly half of peers were privately educated, compared with just 7% of the wider population. Around one third went to Oxford or Cambridge, compared with just 1% nationally. And 11% attended some of Britain’s most elite schools, where annual fees can now top £60,000.

Our conclusion? The Lords is not merely wealthy, it is an institution steeped in economic, educational and social privilege. Yet remarkably little is known about the extent of this wealth. Disclosure requirements remain limited, leaving many of the peers’ financial interests hidden from public view.

And that matters. Membership of the Lords can sit alongside extremely lucrative private-sector careers. Several peers, for example, declared earning between £100,000 and £300,000 a year from company directorships and advisory positions – on top of their parliamentary roles and Lords allowances (a £371 daily rate).
Aristocrats have gone – but privilege has not

This is the paradox at the heart of the modern House of Lords. The old aristocracy may be disappearing from the red benches, but wealth and privilege have not disappeared with it. The aristocracy has increasingly given way to what we termed an “assetocracy” – members of the new financial elite whose power rests on property, finance and accumulated asset-based wealth.

Reforming the second chamber has previously been tied to either removing the aristocratic hereditary peers or (ostensibly) increasing the scope for non-elite appointments. This is primarily done through the House of Lords Appointments Commission and the introduction of crossbenchers, whose appointment does not depend on prime ministerial patronage or political donations.

Yet while these efforts appeared to be producing a diverse collection of Lords through the early 2000s, the trend was reversed with the arrival of the Conservative governments of the 2010s. Since then, my research shows that the second chamber has seen a striking influx of the new “assetocratic” elite.
Appointments of peers with shareholdings over £100,000 (by political party)

My research also reveals a small but clear relationship between wealth and participation in the Lords. Previous accounts have shown that some political donors appear to treat a peerage as a status symbol, playing little part in the day-to-day work of the House. My findings suggest however, that the pattern extends beyond political donors. On average, the wealthiest peers tend to attend less, speak less and contribute less to the work of the House.

One of the book’s central conclusions is that the rise of the assetocrats in the Lords coincided with a wider transformation of British society. It was a period when wealth inequality grew and asset ownership became an increasingly important source of economic advantage.

The Lords did not create these changes, nor are its members the only or primary beneficiaries. But my research shows how peers have often sought to narrow the terms of political debate around wealth and redistribution. They have defended a system that privileges asset ownership and particular forms of wealth accumulation.

For example, Lord Leigh of Hurley, a Conservative peer and businessman, told the House in 2025 that “we need to teach kids that so-called ‘earned income’ is paid, weekly or monthly, without any risk whatever, while ‘unearned income’ is typically generated from an investment, which involves risk to capital and, therefore, deserves greater reward”.

The research points to three conclusions. The first may seem paradoxical, but the more I researched the Lords, the more convinced I became that – certainly on issues beyond wealth and inequality – it is a remarkable source of expertise that often improves and strengthens legislation. That is why abolishing the Lords would throw away an institution that still performs an important democratic function.

Second, reform is nonetheless overdue. Prime ministerial patronage should be curtailed; minimum expectations for attendance and participation introduced; transparency over financial affairs should be increased; and outside employment more tightly regulated where it creates conflicts of interest.

But there is a bigger issue. The transformation of the Lords reflects a much more profound transformation of society. Over the past five decades, the UK has become an economy in which owning property, shares and other assets is an increasingly important route to extraordinary wealth. Removing the last vestiges of the old aristocracy from the Lords will not solve the problem. The deeper challenge is confronting the structural forces that have allowed a new asset-owning elite to take its place.

articles.title: Four ways cities can help protect democratic values
articles.author: Marta Wojciechowska, Lecturer in Politics, King's College London
paras: When people think about democracy, they tend to think about national elections, parliaments or the policies of national governments. Even the recent byelection in Holborn and St Pancras showed that democratic events are often framed around what they mean for the fortunes of national leaders, rather than what they mean for daily life within a community.

But this focus on the national level and on the procedures associated with democracy is shortsighted. Our work, bringing together political theory and local politics, is aimed at developing a deeper understanding of democracy. This is particularly important when democracies around the world are coming under threat from authoritarian leaders and insurgent populist movements.
We argue that politics at the local level, especially in cities, has a critical role to play in resisting authoritarianism. But what can cities do to promote democracy?
1. Standing up to authoritarianism
Cities have long had a strong connection to democratic values. The practices of self-governance in the city-states of ancient Greece or Renaissance Italy bore this out.

Today, cities often provide a progressive counterweight to reactionary and authoritarian politics at the national level. In the US, for example, residents in the city of Minneapolis rose up to resist deportations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials. And in India, gen-Z “cockroach” protests centred on Delhi are challenging alleged electoral fraud and government corruption.

But cities are not inherently democratic. Many elect authoritarian mayors, or enact regressive policies targeted against migrants or LGBTQ+ rights. And urban politics often fails to live up to democratic ideals by sidelining the voices of citizens and exacerbating economic inequality or feelings of social exclusion.

These dynamics can contribute to rising xenophobia and anti-democratic sentiment at the national level. So to understand why cities matter for democracy, it is important to look beyond the outcomes of elections or the agendas of individual mayors or civic movements. Instead, the deeper, more complex and often mundane ways that cities can promote democracy are what really count.
2. Challenging top-down politics

The everyday practices of governance within cities can play an important role in resisting authoritarianism and strengthening democracy. Technocratic forms of governance (that is, those that are top down and led by experts) still tend to dominate. But many cities are challenging this. They are using their legal and political autonomy to experiment with approaches that help to democratise local politics.

For example, they can give greater decision-making power to citizens by engaging them directly in policymaking at the local level. This could be through citizens’ assemblies or letting them play a role in planning the local budget. In turn, urban citizens organising themselves in communities or movements can strengthen democracy from the bottom up.
3. More economic influence for citizens

Urban economics is still generally dominated by the pursuit of growth. This can end up giving the private sector significant power over a city’s future. But some cities are experimenting with alternative approaches.

For example, community wealth building has been adopted in cities such as Cleveland, Ohio, in the US and Preston in the UK. This model promotes community-owned businesses, worker cooperatives, community banks and local control of land and real estate. By engaging citizens in economic decision-making, cities can nurture local democratic culture.
4. Providing the space to organise

Democracy is something that cuts across all aspects of urban life. This includes relations with formal institutions, such as councils. But it also takes in everyday aspects of city living, such as citizens’ relationships with the public spaces in their area.

Physical space within cities is increasingly being commercialised and privatised. But public spaces continue to be important for democratic culture. People use them to protest and put pressure on national and local governments, as happened during housing protests in cities across Spain.
The shared space of urban life can also encourage new forms of political and even moral community. These can push back against the polarisation often associated with national politics.

In an age of rising authoritarianism, urban policymakers can support democracy across multiple dimensions. Cities can certainly democratise government and economic institutions. But their most important contribution may be providing the space and support for citizens to affirm democratic values in their everyday lives.

articles.title: How we mark our ballot paper can affect how we feel about voting. Here’s why
articles.author: João V. Ferreira, Associate Professor in Economics, University of Southampton
paras: Have you ever left a polling station feeling that your mark on the ballot paper didn’t quite say what you wanted it to? Perhaps you liked two candidates but had to drop one, or backed the one who might actually win over the one you preferred.
Our feelings about democracy are important. Who wins matters, and so does whether an election feels fair. But there is another, less obvious factor: what the ballot paper allows us to say.

In his first party conference speech as prime minister, Andy Burnham announced a national commission on electoral reform and promised that Labour’s next manifesto will contain a pledge to change the voting system. Public opinion is moving his way: about 53% of voters now support a change, up from 27% in 2011.

The commission will debate whether votes should translate into seats more proportionately, and which electoral system might achieve that. But a second question deserves a place at the table: what are voters actually asked to do in the voting booth?

Putting one cross next to one name, ranking candidates or ticking every candidate you’d be happy with are very different ways of expressing political preferences. Under “pick one”, any voter who likes several candidates has no way to say so. A single cross records your first choice – not who else you would support, nor how strongly you feel.
This matters to anyone who has ever voted tactically, who felt their vote did not reflect what they think, or who stayed at home on polling day because no single option spoke for them.

The alternatives – approving multiple options or ranking candidates, for example – are known as “smarter ballots”. These deserve serious consideration in any debate on electoral reform, as they could bring both benefits and risks.

In a 2020 study I conducted with colleagues, we asked 1,977 people living in the UK to vote on COVID lockdown policies. When asked to pick just one option, only 2% were able to cast a ballot that matched their true preferences. When using a “smarter ballot” that allowed them to express more preferences, 72% were able to make a choice that corresponded to what they wanted to say.

Research on elections has yielded similar results. In field experiments in two German elections, around 2,400 voters cast their official ballot, with one vote for a candidate and one for a party. They then filled in an “approval ballot”, where they could back as many as they liked. Roughly four out of five people used that freedom to back more than one candidate or party. Today’s methods may therefore be doing a poor job of capturing what the electorate wants.

If you could better express what you think, you might feel more satisfied with your vote – in principle, at least. Yet some people appear to have a taste for simpler voting rules and to stick with what they know. The latter tendency is known as “status quo bias”.

In the German study, one voter who had backed the same party for years asked the researchers why they should change their voting behaviour. Status quo bias is particularly acute among older citizens, who are typically used to established electoral rules and may resist change.

However, smarter ballots appear to appeal to young people, as well as to politically sophisticated voters. The UK’s own history fits this pattern. The 2011 AV referendum asked UK voters whether they wanted to switch to the “alternative vote” system, where voters rank candidates in order of preference. The proposal lost heavily, but about 48% of 18 to 34-year-olds voted Yes, against 30% of those aged 35 to 65 and 19% of those older.
Ballots can change results
In 2012, in experiments across three French cities, 2,340 voters tried out smarter ballots where they could approve or grade several candidates.

France’s usual two-round system favoured “exclusive” candidates – those who are strongly liked by some voters and strongly disliked by others. The smarter ballots, however, favoured “inclusive” candidates who win broader support. In other words, the smarter ballots favoured broadly acceptable candidates, and pushed polarising ones down the list.

The German experiments point the same way. In Konstanz, the left-libertarian Pirate Party won just 4% of the official votes in the polling stations tested, but 21% of participants approved of it when using approval ballots. The Greens topped the approval vote, while the official winner, the CDU, fell to third in this alternative poll.

Transposing this on to a UK by-election, it’s possible to picture a race where Labour, the Liberal Democrats and the Greens split the vote on the centre and left. As a result, a right-leaning candidate could win with just a third of the votes. With approval ballots, the outcome could be different. Supporters could back all three of the centre and left options, and the winner might be more broadly acceptable to a larger share of the electorate.

Smarter ballots might even increase turnout: voters who feel heard may be less likely to stay at home on polling day. My experimental evidence hints at this, but it needs to be tested in real elections.

There is a real tension at play here. Rules that let voters express their views with more nuance than a single vote may run contrary to what they feel comfortable with, because some voters have a taste for simplicity and for what they already know. Tactical voting, which already exists under “pick one”, may take new forms too.
For smarter ballots to work for more than a small part of the electorate, and to overcome status quo bias, they may need to be easy to use and introduced gradually.

But the benefits for democracy could be significant: better representation of voters’ views, less polarising results, higher voter satisfaction and, potentially, higher turnout. To understand these potential benefits and risks, we need more evidence, ideally from real UK elections.

Whatever the electoral reform commission decides, it should look beyond proportional representation and ask what voters are actually being invited to say. Next time you are handed a ballot paper, ask yourself: does this piece of paper let me say what I really think?
